_about: Fact-check DEVELOPMENT set (2026-10-25): 40 answers on 8 fictional projects for tuning the fact check only. 'false_claim' marks whether the answer states a clearly false general technical fact. Correct answers deliberately include true-but-nuanced claims, loosely worded true mechanisms, and statements about the candidate's own design - the cases that caused false alarms. Tiers follow the usual 0-4 rubric.

notesync.title: NoteSync - Collaborative Notes App
notesync.summary: Real-time collaborative notes app using React, Node.js and Yjs CRDTs over WebSockets, with documents persisted in PostgreSQL and offline edits merged on reconnect.

imgresize.title: PixelPipe - Image Resizing Service
imgresize.summary: Serverless image resizing on AWS Lambda triggered by S3 uploads; thumbnails cached behind CloudFront; written in Python with Pillow.

fraudml.title: FraudLens - Card Fraud Detector
fraudml.summary: Gradient-boosted (XGBoost) model flagging fraudulent card transactions on a highly imbalanced dataset (0.2% fraud); evaluated with precision-recall AUC; served with FastAPI.

authsvc.title: KeyGate - OAuth Login Service
authsvc.summary: Login service supporting Google sign-in via OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow with PKCE; issues short-lived JWT access tokens and rotating refresh tokens stored in Redis.

searchbar.title: QuickFind - Autocomplete Search Bar
searchbar.summary: Product-search autocomplete for a campus store: React front end with debounced requests, a Trie-based suggestion service in Go, top suggestions cached in memory.

loadtest.title: Internship - Backend Intern at TicketHub
loadtest.summary: Backend intern (May-July 2025) on the ticket-booking API; load-tested with k6, added database indexes and Redis caching to the seat-availability endpoint (Java, Spring Boot, MySQL).

chatbot.title: StudyBuddy - Course Q&A Bot
chatbot.summary: Answers questions about course notes using retrieval-augmented generation: notes chunked and embedded with a sentence-transformer, stored in ChromaDB, answers generated by an LLM with cited chunks.

drone.title: SkyMap - Drone Mapping Pipeline
drone.summary: Stitches drone photos into orthomosaic maps using OpenCV feature matching (ORB) and homographies; GPS tags used to order images; processed on a GPU workstation.

items.question: Why did you use a CRDT like Yjs instead of operational transform?

answers.answer: With a CRDT every client can apply edits locally and they converge to the same document regardless of the order the updates arrive, so offline edits just merge when someone reconnects. Operational transform usually needs a central server to order and transform operations, which made offline editing harder. The cost is metadata: Yjs keeps tombstones for deleted characters, so documents grow, and I compact them when saving to Postgres.
CRDT updates converge in any order, so offline edits merge on reconnect without a central server deciding the order.
Yjs basically guarantees everyone ends up with the same text, as long as all the updates eventually reach everyone. That's why I didn't need a server to sequence edits.
CRDTs work by locking the paragraph someone is editing, so two people can never edit the same place at the same time, which is why there are no conflicts.
I picked Yjs for offline support. Also CRDTs never store any extra metadata, so the document size stays exactly the same as the plain text.

items.question: How does PixelPipe avoid resizing the same image again and again?

answers.answer: Resizing only happens once per upload: the S3 upload event triggers the Lambda, which writes the thumbnails back to a separate bucket. After that, requests go through CloudFront, so popular thumbnails are served from edge caches and don't even reach S3 most of the time. I set a long cache TTL because the file names include a content hash, so a changed image gets a new URL instead of needing invalidation.
Thumbnails are generated once on upload, then served through CloudFront with long cache times because the file names are content-hashed.
Because the names are content hashes, the same image always maps to the same thumbnail key, so the Lambda just checks whether that key already exists before doing any work.
Lambda functions keep all their memory between every invocation forever, so I stored the resized images in a global variable and they're always there on the next request.
CloudFront caches it. CloudFront also automatically resizes images for every device without any code, so the Lambda is only a backup.

items.question: Why did you evaluate FraudLens with precision-recall AUC instead of accuracy?

answers.answer: With 0.2% fraud, a model that predicts 'not fraud' for everything is 99.8% accurate and useless. ROC AUC also looks flattering on imbalanced data because the huge number of true negatives keeps the false-positive rate low. Precision-recall focuses on the fraud class itself: how many flagged transactions are really fraud and how much fraud we catch. Our PR-AUC was 0.61 against a baseline of 0.002.
At 0.2% fraud, accuracy is 99.8% for a model that never flags anything; PR-AUC measures how well we actually find the fraud.
Accuracy is misleading when one class is tiny. The baseline for PR-AUC is just the fraud rate, so it's a much more honest number here.
PR-AUC is always higher than accuracy, so it makes the model look better in the report, and it doesn't depend on the class balance at all.
Accuracy is bad with imbalance. I also used SMOTE on the test set, which is the correct way to make the evaluation fair.

items.question: Why did KeyGate use PKCE with the authorization code flow?

answers.answer: PKCE protects the authorization code if someone intercepts it. The client makes a random code verifier, sends only its SHA-256 hash with the login request, and has to present the original verifier when exchanging the code for tokens, so a stolen code alone is useless. Our mobile and single-page clients can't keep a client secret safely, which is exactly the case PKCE is for.
Public clients can't keep a secret, so PKCE makes an intercepted authorization code useless without the original code verifier.
In our setup the refresh tokens rotate on every use, so even if one leaks it only works once and then the whole chain is revoked.
PKCE encrypts the access token so nobody can read what's inside a JWT, which is why we didn't need HTTPS for the token endpoint.
PKCE is for public clients. JWTs also can't be decoded by anyone without the secret key, so putting the user's details in them is private.

items.question: How did you keep QuickFind's autocomplete fast?

answers.answer: The front end debounces keystrokes by 150 ms so we don't send a request per character. On the server, product names live in a Trie, so finding everything that starts with a prefix only walks the prefix's characters, not the whole catalogue. Each node keeps its top 5 suggestions precomputed, so a lookup is basically the length of the prefix plus reading five items.
Debounced requests, and a Trie with the top suggestions stored at each node, so a lookup only depends on the prefix length.
A Trie makes prefix lookups roughly proportional to the length of what you typed, which matters more than the catalogue size for us.
Tries are fast because they sort all the words with quicksort every time you type, and debouncing makes the network itself faster.
We used debouncing. A hash map would also give prefix search in O(1) for any prefix, the Trie was just easier to code.

items.question: During your TicketHub internship, how did you speed up the seat-availability endpoint?

answers.answer: k6 showed p95 latency around 1.8 seconds at 200 virtual users. EXPLAIN showed a full table scan on the seats table, so I added a composite index on (event_id, status), which brought the query to a few milliseconds. Then I cached availability per event in Redis with a 5-second TTL, since a slightly stale count is fine for browsing but the booking itself always re-checks the database inside a transaction.
Composite index on (event_id, status) after EXPLAIN showed a full scan, plus a 5-second Redis cache for browsing; booking still checks the database.
The cache is only for showing availability. The actual booking locks the seat rows in a transaction, so the cache can never cause a double booking.
I added an index on every column of every table, because indexes have no cost and make every query faster, including inserts.
I added Redis caching. Redis also guarantees that cached data is always perfectly in sync with MySQL, so there's no staleness.

items.question: How does StudyBuddy find the right part of the notes for a question?

answers.answer: The notes are split into chunks of about 300 tokens with some overlap, and each chunk is embedded with a sentence-transformer and stored in ChromaDB. A question is embedded the same way and we take the top 4 chunks by cosine similarity. The LLM only sees those chunks and must cite them, so students can check the source. Chunk size mattered: big chunks diluted the match, tiny ones lost context.
Notes are chunked and embedded; the question's embedding retrieves the most similar chunks from ChromaDB, which the LLM answers from with citations.
Embeddings put sentences with similar meaning close together, so the search finds relevant chunks even when the student uses different words than the notes.
ChromaDB does keyword matching only, it counts exact word overlaps, and embeddings are just a way to compress the text so it takes less disk space.
We embed chunks in ChromaDB. Because we use RAG, the LLM can never make anything up, so we didn't need citations.

items.question: How does SkyMap stitch the drone photos together?

answers.answer: For each pair of overlapping photos, ORB finds keypoints and descriptors, and we match them with a brute-force Hamming matcher. RANSAC then estimates a homography from the matches while throwing out bad ones, and the image is warped into the shared map frame. GPS tags decide which photos are neighbours, so we only match likely overlaps instead of every pair.
ORB keypoints matched between overlapping photos, a RANSAC homography per pair, then warping into one map; GPS picks which pairs to match.
A homography is fine here because from that height the ground is close to a flat plane; for hilly areas it would distort a bit.
ORB is a deep neural network trained on aerial images, and RANSAC is what blends the colours between photos so the seams disappear.
We used ORB and homographies. A homography can also perfectly correct for hills and buildings of any height, so the map has no distortion.
